title: Stacks, Queues, Monotonic Stacks & Deques
summary: Two of the simplest structures in CS — but once you see the *order* you process things in, a whole family of O(n) interview tricks falls out.

blocks.markdown:
A stack and a queue differ by one rule: which end you take from.

- **Stack** — Last-In-First-Out. Last thing in is first out, like a pile of plates.
- **Queue** — First-In-First-Out. First come, first served, like a coffee line.
- Both do their core moves in **O(1)**: push/pop for a stack, enqueue/dequeue for a queue.
- A **deque** adds and removes at *both* ends in O(1) — a superset of both.
- Giving up random access is the point: it buys the O(1) guarantee.

blocks.subTitle: Which one to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Match the structure to the *order* the problem demands.

| If you need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Most-recent-first, nesting, undo | Stack |
| Fair, in-order, BFS, buffering | Queue |
| Add/remove at both ends | Deque |
| "Next greater/smaller" | Monotonic stack |
| Sliding-window min/max in O(n) | Monotonic deque |

blocks.subTitle: Stack and queue moves
blocks.markdown:
A stack only ever touches one end; a queue touches two.

![Stack push/pop and queue enqueue/dequeue](assets/a05-stacks-queues/stack-queue-ops.svg)

- **Stack** — push, pop, and peek all act on the **top**.
- **Queue** — items enter at the **back** (enqueue) and leave from the **front** (dequeue).
- Each operation is still **O(1)** regardless of how many ends are involved.

blocks.subTitle: Why a queue needs a ring buffer
blocks.markdown:
A stack is easy on an array; a queue is the tricky one.

- A **stack** is just a dynamic array — push/pop at the end is O(1) amortized.
- Removing the **front** of a plain array shifts everything left — that's **O(n)**.
- The fix is a **circular (ring) buffer**: keep `head` and `tail` indices that wrap with modulo. No shifting, so enqueue and dequeue stay O(1).
- A doubly linked list also works, at the cost of pointer overhead.

blocks.subTitle: The monotonic stack
blocks.markdown:
Keep the stack always increasing or decreasing, and an O(n²) scan collapses to O(n).

![Monotonic stack solving next-greater-element](assets/a05-stacks-queues/monotonic-stack-nge.svg)

- Before pushing the current element, **pop everything it beats**.
- The instant you pop something, you've found its answer — the current value is its "next greater".
- Each index is **pushed once and popped once**, so the whole scan is **O(n)** despite the inner `while`.
- In `[2,1,5,3]`, when `5` arrives it pops both `1` and `2` and never re-touches them.

blocks.subTitle: Pattern: Next Greater Element
blocks.markdown:
Memorize this shape — it covers a whole family of "next greater/smaller" problems.

```python
def next_greater(a):
    res = [-1] * len(a)
    stack = []                 # holds INDICES, values decreasing
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        while stack and x > a[stack[-1]]:
            res[stack.pop()] = x
        stack.append(i)
    return res
```

- Store **indices**, not values — you usually need position or distance.
- **O(n)** time, **O(n)** space; indices left on the stack keep `-1`.

blocks.subTitle: Queue from two stacks
blocks.markdown:
A classic interview move: build a FIFO queue out of two LIFO stacks.

- Push every new item onto an **in** stack.
- To dequeue, if the **out** stack is empty, pour the whole `in` stack into `out` — reversing the order.
- Then pop from `out`, which now hands back oldest-first.
- Each element moves at most twice, so dequeue is **amortized O(1)**.

blocks.subTitle: Array vs linked list backing
blocks.markdown:
Both back stacks and queues — they trade speed for stability.

| Aspect | Array / ring buffer | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Cache | Friendly | Scattered |
| Resize | Occasional | Never |
| Per-element | Lean | Pointer overhead |

For interviews and most production code the array/ring-buffer version wins on real-world speed.

blocks.subTitle: Picking the pattern
blocks.markdown:
State the *order* you need, then the structure picks itself.

- **Nesting, matching, undo** (parentheses, expression eval) → **stack**.
- **Order-preserving or level-by-level** (BFS, scheduling) → **queue**.
- **Sliding-window min/max in O(n)** → **monotonic deque** (a heap is O(n log k)).
- **Nested loop scanning left/right for first bigger/smaller** → **monotonic stack**.
- Use the most restrictive structure that fits — it documents intent.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
These structures run the systems you use daily.

- **Call stack** — one frame per active function; LIFO because the newest call must finish first. Blow the limit and you get a **stack overflow** ([a07-recursion-backtracking](a07-recursion-backtracking.md)).
- **Message brokers** — Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ are durable FIFO queues decoupling fast producers from slow consumers ([b06-messaging-streaming](b06-messaging-streaming.md)).
- **Traversal** — BFS uses a queue, DFS uses a stack ([a11-graphs-traversal](a11-graphs-traversal.md)).
- **Undo/redo and browser history** — two stacks each.

blocks.subTitle: Signals in production
blocks.markdown:
Queues are usually the part you watch most closely.

- **Queue depth / backlog** — a steadily growing queue means consumers trail producers; alert on the *rate of change*, not just the value.
- **Time-in-queue** — rising wait time warns before backlog looks alarming; it's the latency users feel.
- **Bounded-queue drops** — a nonzero reject rate means load shedding, intended ([b13-rate-limiting-resilience](b13-rate-limiting-resilience.md)) or a bug.
- **Recursion depth** — runaway recursion crashes with a stack thousands of frames deep.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"A queue is a slow stack."** No — they answer different *orders*; the wrong one runs but returns wrong results.
- **"Dequeue from an array is O(1)."** Only with a ring buffer; naive `removeFirst` shifts everything, turning O(n) into O(n²).
- **Storing values in a monotonic stack.** Usually store **indices** — you need position or distance.
- **Wrong monotonic direction.** "Next greater" → keep it **decreasing**; write the invariant before coding.
- **Popping an empty stack.** Always guard the access.
